title: What data architecture is
summary: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change; this chapter shows how to find them, weigh them against quality attributes and write them down.

blocks.text: 1.1 Architecture versus engineering

Data engineering builds and runs pipelines: it writes the ingestion job, the dbt model, the Airflow DAG, the alert that fires when a load is late. Data architecture decides the shape those pipelines live in: which systems exist, how data moves between them, where the source of truth sits, who owns what, and which guarantees the platform gives its consumers.

A useful working definition: **architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse**. Choosing a column name in a staging model is engineering. Choosing whether the company stores analytical data in an open table format on object storage or inside a proprietary warehouse is architecture, because undoing it later means migrating petabytes, rewriting jobs and retraining teams.

head: Concern
Engineering question
Architecture question
rows: Ingestion
How do I load this table incrementally?
Do we use CDC, batch extracts or events as the default integration style?

Which partition column for this table?

Is there a semantic layer? Which latency do we promise to whom?

blocks.text: 1.2 Quality attributes

Requirements come in two kinds. **Functional requirements** say what the system must produce: a daily revenue table, a fraud score per transaction. **Quality attributes** (non-functional requirements) say how well: how fast, how cheap, how reliably, how safely. Architecture is mostly about quality attributes, because almost any architecture can produce the revenue table; they differ in what it costs and how it fails.

head: Attribute
What it means for data
Typical measure
rows: Scalability
Handles growth in volume, velocity, users and number of pipelines
Cost and runtime per extra TB or per extra source
Latency / freshness
Time from an event happening to it being queryable
Seconds (streaming), minutes (micro-batch), hours (daily batch)
Query performance
Time for a consumer query to return
p95 dashboard query under a few seconds
Cost
Storage, compute, egress and people time
Monthly spend, cost per query, cost per pipeline
Reliability
Data arrives, is complete and correct, and recovers from failure
Freshness SLA hit rate, mean time to recovery
Governance
Access control, lineage, privacy, auditability
Time to answer *who can see column X*, erasure turnaround
Evolvability
Ease of adding sources, changing schemas, swapping engines
Lead time for a new source; blast radius of a schema change

blocks.text: These attributes pull against each other. Lower latency raises cost and operational complexity. Stronger governance adds friction to evolvability. The architect's job is to make the trade explicit and choose deliberately, rather than discover it in production.
Asking stakeholders *how fresh does the data need to be?* almost always gets *real time*. Ask instead what decision the data feeds and how often that decision is made.
1.3 Reversible and irreversible decisions

A practical way to spend design effort is to sort decisions into **one-way doors** (hard to reverse) and **two-way doors** (cheap to reverse). Spend analysis, prototypes and review on one-way doors; make two-way door decisions quickly and revisit them when you learn more.

head: Usually hard to reverse
Usually easy to reverse
rows: Storage and table format for the core analytical data
Which BI tool a team uses for one dashboard
Primary integration pattern (CDC vs batch extracts vs events)
Scheduling time of a nightly job
Grain and keys of core fact tables
Naming of an intermediate model
Data residency and retention policy once data is shared
Warehouse size for a given workload
Contracts published to many consumers
Internal transformation logic behind a stable contract

blocks.text: Good architecture also *converts* one-way doors into two-way doors. Open file and table formats reduce engine lock-in. A stable published contract (a view or a semantic model) lets the team change everything behind it. Each costs a little now to buy optionality later.
Optionality is not free. Building every component to be swappable produces a platform that is generic, slow to deliver and hard to understand. Pay for reversibility where the uncertainty is real.
1.4 Gathering requirements
Most failed data platforms did not fail on technology. They answered a question nobody asked, or missed a constraint (a regulator, a budget, a skills gap) that surfaced late.

items: **Consumers and decisions**: who reads the data, what decisions or products it feeds, and what happens if it is late or wrong.
**Sources**: which systems produce the data, their owners, change rates, volumes, access methods and how stable their schemas are.
**Quality attributes**: freshness, query latency, availability, and a budget range. Get numbers, even rough ones.
**Constraints**: regulation (GDPR, sector rules), data residency, existing contracts with vendors, cloud provider, team size and skills.
**Volumes and growth**: rows per day, total size, number of users and concurrent queries, expected growth over two or three years.
**Ownership**: who runs each component after go-live.

blocks.text: Back-of-envelope sizing is worth doing early. 50 million events per day at 500 bytes each is 25 GB per day raw, roughly 9 TB per year; in Parquet with typical compression that may be 1-3 TB per year. That is small for a cloud warehouse; a large cluster is probably not needed.

blocks.title: Freshness negotiated down
blocks.text: A retail company asked for a real-time sales dashboard. Interviews showed store managers checked it at opening and at lunch, and the finance team needed figures reconciled to the cent by 09:00 the next day.
items: Hourly micro-batch loads met the store managers' need at a fraction of the cost of streaming.
A nightly reconciled table met the finance requirement with stronger checks.
The ADR recorded the trigger to revisit: a business case for intraday stock rebalancing.

blocks.text: 1.5 Architecture decision records

An **architecture decision record (ADR)** is a short Markdown file in a repository that captures one significant decision: context, options, choice and consequences. ADRs are numbered and immutable; when a decision changes, a new ADR supersedes the old one rather than editing it.

blocks.title: docs/adr/0007-table-format.md
blocks.text:
# ADR 0007: Use Apache Iceberg as the table format for the lakehouse

Status: Accepted (supersedes ADR 0003)
Date: 2026-03-04

## Context
Three engines (Spark, Trino, Snowflake) need to read and write the same
curated tables. Plain Parquet directories give no atomic commits and
listing large prefixes is slow.

## Options
1. Plain Parquet + Hive metastore
2. Delta Lake
3. Apache Iceberg

## Decision
Iceberg, with a REST catalog.

## Consequences
+ Atomic commits, schema and partition evolution, multi-engine reads.
- Table maintenance (compaction, snapshot expiry) becomes our job.
- Revisit if the chosen catalog does not support a required engine.
ADRs pay off months later, when someone asks why the platform looks the way it does. Without them, decisions are either relitigated endlessly or never questioned at all.

blocks.title: Lifecycle of an architecture decision
blocks.caption: Record the trigger that would make you reconsider; it turns a fixed decision into a monitored one.

blocks.text: 1.6 The shape of this trail

The trail follows decisions in the order an architect meets them: lifecycle, formats, storage, compute and time (2-6), modelling (7-11), layers (12-15), ingestion (16-20), Iceberg and Snowflake (21-29), operations and semantics (30-36), then reference architectures and cases (37-49).

blocks.title: Classify the decisions
blocks.text: A mid-size insurer is building its first analytics platform. List ten decisions the team must make in the next quarter (for example cloud provider, ingestion tool, warehouse sizing, modelling style, BI tool, naming conventions). For each, classify it as a one-way or two-way door, name the quality attribute it most affects, and say which ones deserve an ADR.
hints: Ask what it would cost in weeks of work to reverse each decision in two years.
Decisions that many consumers depend on are harder to reverse than internal ones.

items: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse; engineering works inside them.
Quality attributes (scalability, latency, cost, reliability, governance, evolvability) drive architecture and trade off against each other.
Spend design effort on one-way doors; use open formats and stable contracts to make doors reversible where uncertainty is real.
Gather requirements from decisions and constraints, with rough numbers for volume, freshness and budget.
Record significant decisions in ADRs, including the trigger that would justify revisiting them.

blocks.q: Which of these is most clearly an architectural decision rather than an engineering one?
options: Changing the schedule of a nightly job from 02:00 to 03:00
Choosing CDC as the default way to integrate operational databases
Renaming a column in a staging model
Adding an index hint to a slow query
blocks.explain: The integration style shapes every downstream pipeline and is expensive to change later. The other options are local and cheap to reverse.

blocks.q: A stakeholder asks for real-time data. What is the best next step?
options: Ask which decision the data supports and how often that decision is made
Explain that real time is too expensive
Design a streaming pipeline, since real time was requested
Offer hourly batch as a compromise without further discussion
blocks.explain: Freshness should follow from the decision cadence. Building streaming by default overspends; refusing or compromising blindly may miss a genuine low-latency need.

blocks.q: What should happen to an ADR when the decision it records is changed?
options: Move it to an archive folder without a replacement
Write a new ADR that supersedes it and mark the old one as superseded
Edit it in place so it reflects the current state
blocks.explain: ADRs are an immutable log. Superseding keeps the history of why decisions were made; editing in place loses the original context.

blocks.q: Which practice most directly turns a one-way door into a two-way door?
options: Running all jobs from a single orchestrator
Adding more compute to the warehouse
Writing longer documentation for each pipeline
Publishing a stable contract (view or semantic model) in front of internal tables
blocks.explain: A stable contract decouples consumers from internals, so the team can change storage or logic behind it. More compute or documentation does not reduce the cost of reversing a decision.
